items.abstract: Social naturalism about moral responsibility is a position developed by Pamela Hieronymi on the basis of P. F. Strawson’s work. The view has been criticized by, among others, Stephen Darwall and Paul Russell, mainly because it seems to lead to an objectionable form of relativism about moral responsibility. My aim is to explain how the social naturalist could respond to the charge of objectionable relativism without losing some crucial social naturalist insights, including an emphasis on our social nature and the contingency of our moral practices, and a dynamic view of human capacities and standards of regard. I conclude that social naturalists can only avoid objectionable relativism by giving up on some ideas that have been thought central to social naturalism, such as the idea that incapacity for morally responsible agency cannot be the universal condition and the idea that the conditions of moral responsibility dynamically adjust to the statistically ordinary capacities in a society. Social naturalists will also have to rethink their response to the incompatibilist.
items.title: Dynamic Social Naturalism Without Objectionable Relativism About Moral Responsibility

items.abstract: An expressivist logic is a logical system that conservatively extends an atomic material (potentially defeasible) consequence relation to logically complex one where properties of the atomic and extended consequence relation itself are codified (expressed) by logical operators of the system. A paradigmatic instance of such expressive operators is a conditional satisfying the so-called Deduction-Detachment theorem (Γ |~ A → B iff Γ, A |~ B), where the conditional (A → B) expresses that if its antecedent is added to the premise set (i.e., if we suppose it), then its consequent follows from the premise set thus expanded. In this paper, we extend the expressive power of the currently state-of-the-art expressivist logical system, NonMonotonic MultiSuccedent Sequent Calculus, by expanding it with a new logical operator, ↓ → , that plays the opposite expressive role to that of conditional: Γ |~ A ↓ → B iff Γ－{A} |~ B. The new conditional A ↓ → B, which we call downward-facing conditional, expresses that if its antecedent is subtracted from the premise set (i.e., if we bracket it), then its consequent follows from the premise set thus shrunk. We argue that the addition of this new operator strengthens the expressive power of the resulting system to the extreme that we call holographic monadologicality, where the consequence set of an arbitrary premise set contains all the information about the consequence set of every other premise set.
items.title: A Holographic Monadologic: Introducing Downward-Facing Conditionals

items.abstract: I explore how Kantian forms of constitutivism like Rational Constitutivism can deal with the best-known objection to constitutivism – namely, Enoch’s “schmagency objection”. In discussing this, I hope to draw out how a capacity-theoretic version of constitutivism like Rational Constitutivism provides us with additional resources for responding to such objections, through discussion of the relevance to this objection of the connection between understanding and self-understanding that is fundamental to such views. I also discuss how the “schmagency objection” is best understood, and the conditions on it, if it is to be compelling in this context.
items.title: The Fate of Schmeason

items.abstract: Abstract Contemporary political philosophy has devoted extensive attention to technology, risk, and governance, yet it has paid little attention to the role of everyday material practices in shaping political virtue under industrial conditions. This paper argues that an increased degree of self-sufficiency, understood as domain-sensitive reduction of market reliance, should be recovered as a political virtue for technologically mediated societies. While acknowledging the benefits of industrial society like abundance and health security, the paper diagnoses how large-scale production and radical division of labour generate social exploitation, ecological harm, and individual alienation. Calibrated self-sufficiency is defended as a practical response that reduces social and ecological complicity while preserving opportunities for materially engaged agency and forms of activity that may be conducive to flourishing. The argument frames self-sufficiency as a context-sensitive optimization strategy, demonstrating that this orientation is universalizable without requiring social withdrawal or technological regression.
items.title: Self-Sufficiency as a Political Virtue: Agency and Responsibility in the Age of Technology

items.abstract: Abstract This paper argues that large language models (LLMs) and related technical systems are neither morally neutral instruments nor candidate bearers of virtue, but components of larger systems to which virtue terms can sometimes be applied. Drawing on virtue ethics, 4E cognition, and work on human–AI coevolution, it develops a three-level framework that distinguishes scaffolded , extended , and distributed virtue, and it specifies membership conditions under which a technical system becomes part of a virtue-bearing assemblage without thereby becoming virtuous itself. The framework is applied to an extended case study of justificatory practice in a regulatory agency, and three defeasible diagnostic indicators—removal, attribution, and correction—are proposed, to be applied jointly with those conditions in determining at which level a given sociotechnical arrangement operates. The paper further argues that alignment is better described as pseudo-habituation than as habituation: it reproduces the external profile of Aristotelian ethismos while lacking its constitutive features, and this disanalogy is precisely what blocks the ascription of virtue to models. The same coupling mechanisms that can stabilise epistemic and political virtues can entrench corresponding vices, and the paper closes with the governance implications of this ambivalence.
items.title: Extended Virtues: From Human Character to Sociotechnical Moral Ecologies

items.abstract: Abstract The deeper threat of AI technology to democracy does not consist merely in the abuse of the rules of fair elections, the use of fake material in the election campaign, or fraudulent election results, but in the subversion of the fundamental principles of a democratic regime: political participation, adequate representation and the very authority of the ensuing government. The thesis of the article is that there are no moral or political experts – human or artificial (algorithmic)—and that the delegation of the power to make political decisions to AI contradicts the basic liberal claim that the final arbiter of moral and political decisions is the individual human agent who autonomously and conscientiously takes personal responsibility. No sophisticated algorithm can truly represent our individuality and actual choice, since we are free to change our past attitudes and values which served as the basis for the algorithmic choice made on our behalf. Thus, even if we can in principle envisage a political community which is managed better by AI than by the existing human procedure, the value of both personal autonomy and of the traditional civic virtue of democratic engagement is superior to a computationally organized political order which would mean the loss of human agency. If human beings are “political animals”, then the cooperative enterprise of choosing a truly representative government, based on public Habermasian discourse, negotiations, grouping under parties and assuming responsibility cannot be replaced by a super-human – even an impartial, fair and efficient – algorithmic procedure.
items.title: Can Political Choice Be Delegated to AI? Conscientiousness as Constitutive of Civic Virtue

items.abstract: Contemporary theories of gender terms typically give explanatory priority to meaning and truth-conditions. This paper develops an alternative approach, force contextualism, drawing on Talia Mae Bettcher’s attention to trans linguistic practices and an underexplored aspect of Charles Travis’s occasion-sensitivity: the dependence of illocutionary force on the practical projects or “games” in which utterances function. On this view, gender locutions may function as assertions, avowals, prescriptions, or other acts, and may perform several such roles simultaneously. I develop a game-relative account of assertion on which speakers make themselves answerable for things being as represented, thereby becoming exposed to the risk of error. Applying the account to transphobic, medical, trans-community, and crisis-centre contexts shows how the practical point and values of a game bear on the force of gender locutions. The framework also opens an ameliorative question: which games, classifications, and values ought to structure our practices?
items.title: Force Contextualism and Gender Terms

items.abstract: The epistemic dimension of safe spaces has been studied through the concepts of epistemic injustice and epistemic oppression, emphasizing the credibility deficits experienced by historically marginalized groups. Drawing on Bondy’s ( 2010 ) concept of argumentative injustice, we propose an analysis of the argumentative component of these spaces in order to contribute to the formalization of their epistemic dimension and identification of instances in which epistemic agency may be inhibited or enhanced. This implies that safe spaces are not disconnected from a concern for truth, as is sometimes claimed. To this end, we first analyze how ad hominem fallacies grounded in identity-based prejudices operate by discrediting an interlocutor’s argument, undermining their subsequent credibility, and deteriorating their argumentative self-efficacy, thereby creating an epistemically and argumentatively unsafe space. Second, we show how legitimate ad verecundiam arguments can contribute to the construction of epistemically safe spaces. Additionally, we argue that there are ad verecundiam fallacies by excessive credibility attributed on the basis of membership in privileged social groups, resulting in forms of argumentative injustice. We illustrate how this operates in the cases of overmedicalization of childbirth, authority bias in Milgram’s experiments, and the rise of Lysenko in Soviet biology. We conclude that attending to the argumentative dimension of safe spaces makes it possible to identify and correct distortions in deliberation that affect not only marginalized groups, but also the epistemic community as a whole.
items.title: The Epistemic and Argumentative Dimensions of Safe Spaces

items.abstract: When engaging with each other, discussants navigate a complex set of communicative norms that aim at a variety of goals. Communicators may for example choose to be reasonable, polite, funny, persuasive, or just. Pursuing several goals simultaneously may lead to normative tensions. This essay addresses the relationship and potential areas of conflict between the rules of reasonableness (in the pragma-dialectical version) and ethical norms. To that end it first explores synergies between both sets of rules before concentrating on four possible tensions. These may be expected between either Kantian or Utilitarian ethics and four of the pragma-dialectical commandments: the Freedom rule (#1), the Obligation-to-defend rule (#2), the Relevance rule (#4), or the Concluding rule (#9). Finally, the essay addresses three recent implicit or explicit challenges posed against the pragma-dialectical rules: Kristie Dotson’s “ Tracking Epistemic Violence , Tracking Practices of Silencing ” ( 2011 ), Beth Innocenti’s “ Demanding a Halt to Metadiscussions ” ( 2022 ) and Katharina Stevens’ “ Standing Norms in Argumentation ” ( 2025 ). It concludes that while there are important aspects of normative tension between reasonableness and justice, none of them raises to a full conflict or contradiction.
items.title: Is it reasonable to be just?

items.abstract: This article introduces the notion of “theology of the algorithm” as an interpretive framework for understanding contemporary transformations in the relationship between technology, transcendence, and authority in digital societies. Starting from an account of secularization not as the mere disappearance of religion, but as the transformation and relocation of its symbolic functions, the article argues that algorithms increasingly assume roles functionally analogous to attributes traditionally associated with the divine: omniscience, omnipresence, predictive power, judgment, and a soteriological function. The article also traces this process to the capacity of digital technologies to address fundamental anthropological concerns related to memory, mortality, and the search for meaning. The theoretical core of the article interprets this new form of secularized transcendence through Feuerbach’s concept of alienation. Just as, in religion, human beings project their own qualities onto an entity subsequently perceived as autonomous and superior, so, in the digital sphere, collectively produced cognitive, mnemonic, and predictive capacities are embodied in algorithmic systems and perceived as independent of their creators. On this basis, the article develops the notion of “algorithmic disalienation”: a critical reappropriation of the human, social, and historical origins of algorithms, aimed at promoting transparency, responsibility, and democratic control over digital technologies
items.journal: Journal of Ethics and Emerging Technologies
items.title: Theology of the Algorithm

items.abstract: Abstract Choices that affect how well off future people will be often also affect who they will be. This generates “the Non-Identity Problem”: the problem of explaining why it would be wrong to create someone whose life would be worth living, rather than a numerically non-identical person whose life would be better. A growing number of contractualists say that their theory solves this problem, and to great effect. Contractualism is uniquely positioned to demonstrate that the choice at issue would be wrong because it would wrong someone, and thus to deliver an attractive, non-consequentialist theory of intergenerational ethics. I argue this is a mistake. Contractualism can neither solve the Non-Identity Problem nor deliver the theory of intergenerational ethics promised. This conclusion proves consequential not only for contractualist moral theory, but for intergenerational ethics, generally.
items.title: Contractualism and Two Types of Non-Identity
One Life to Lead: The Mysteries of Time and the Goods of Attachment, Written by Samuel Scheffler
